AM13I-01.note: Two unit-rate divisions plus a cents conversion; all three distractors are real methods (per-ounce of the wrong bottle, price difference over 64, price difference over the ounce difference).

AM13I-02.note: Two direct steps. Only 1,575 (subtracting 45 donors instead of 45x24) is a method error; 660 and 720 are bare numbers.

AM13I-03.note: One product, no reasoning at all - the only failure modes are 52 weeks, 40 hours, or dropping the $0.40. Difficulty here is keystrokes, not thought.

AM13I-04.note: Two conversions each with a direction decision; every distractor is one of the three wrong choices (skip a factor, divide by 1.15 instead of multiply).

AM13I-06.note: Single rate inversion. 405 is the multiply-instead-of-divide trap; 675 and 702 do not correspond to any method I can construct, so the item is effectively two-choice for a solver who catches the inversion.

AM13I-07.note: Good kind of hard-in-miniature: the natural first approach is the full rectangle perimeter, which lands exactly on 702, and remembering the gate but not the building gives 675, remembering the building but not the gate gives 486.

AM13I-08.note: Volume-density-then-compare chain is honest, but 8,448 (stopping at the load mass) and 3,720 (treating 5.28 cubic metres as 5,280 kg) are the only real methods; the work is more arithmetic than decision.

AM13I-09.note: Mass-to-length then a floor. 45 is the stop-short trap and 8 the wrong-pairing trap; the 'whole pieces' floor is the discriminating step and no distractor rewards rounding up, which is a small miss.

AM13I-10.note: The good kind of hard: the natural first approach lands exactly on distractors - 35.0 is 15+20 and 32.0 is the compounded fall read as the required rise. The student must invert 0.68 rather than negate it.

AM13I-11.note: Requires setting up an unstated inverse relation (chairs scale as budget/price) and then flooring 151.2. 144 is the clean trap for handling the 25 percent price rise but ignoring the budget rise; 141 and 214 are weaker.

AM13I-12.note: Standard two-rate system, but it asks for distance and not time, so 121 catches the solver who reports the wrong leg; 160 is equal-time and 132.5 is half the distance.
